title: Types of Financing
outcomes: Classify financial needs and match them with suitable sources.
Compare equity, preference shares, retained earnings, debentures and bonds and compute EPS under alternative plans.
Explain term loans, bridge finance, venture capital, securitisation and lease financing.
Describe short-term sources, bank credit and export finance.
Explain other, international and contemporary sources of finance.

meta.exam_tip: Frequent theory: lease types, venture capital methods, securitisation, bridge finance, export finance, ADR/GDR and ESG bonds; keep definitions crisp.

concepts.title: Financial needs and matching sources
body: A business needs funds for three periods: long-term (generally beyond 5–10 years — fixed assets and the permanent part of working capital), medium-term (more than a year up to 5 years) and short-term (up to a year — stock, debtors, cash).

Matching principle: finance short-term needs from short-term sources, medium-term needs from medium-term sources and long-term needs from long-term sources. Funding a factory with a 90-day loan creates refinancing risk; funding stock with equity is costly.
The stage of the business also matters: high-uncertainty start-ups depend on equity (angels, venture capital); stable firms can carry more debt.
Sources can be classified by basic source (share capital, debt, internal funds), by maturity (long, medium, short) and by ownership and control (owned vs borrowed).
concepts.analogy: Match the loan to the life of what it buys — you would not take a 20-year home loan to pay this month's grocery bill, nor buy a house with a credit card.
concepts.work: Banks ask for the "means of finance" for a project and check that long-term assets are not funded with short-term borrowings.

concepts.title: Equity and preference share capital
body: Equity (ordinary) shares are permanent capital. Equity holders bear the highest risk, are paid dividends only after all other claims (an appropriation of profit, not a charge), and in winding up get what remains after others are paid. So they expect the highest return — equity is the costliest source.

Merits of equity: no repayment obligation; no compulsory dividend; widens the capital base and so supports further borrowing; more can be raised later through a rights issue. Demerits: dilutes EPS and control of existing holders; investors see it as risky.
Kinds of equity issue include a fresh issue, a rights issue, bonus shares and sweat equity.

Preference shares get priority over equity for a fixed dividend and for capital repayment in winding up. They are hybrid: like equity, the dividend is not tax-deductible; like debt, the rate is fixed. They are usually cumulative and redeemable; cumulative convertible preference shares convert into equity after some years and suit long-gestation projects.

Merits of preference shares: no EPS dilution, leverage benefit, no takeover risk (limited voting), redeemable. Demerits: dividend gives no tax shield, so costlier than debt; arrears block equity dividends and hurt reputation.
concepts.analogy: Equity holders are the owners at the back of the queue who keep whatever is left; preference holders stand in front with a fixed ticket; lenders stand at the very front.
concepts.work: Start-ups issue equity; mature companies use preference shares when they want funds without giving up votes.

concepts.title: Retained earnings, debentures and bonds
body: Retained earnings (ploughing back profits): belong to equity holders, raise net worth, need no issue cost, dilute no control and carry almost no risk. Whether to retain depends on whether the firm can earn more than shareholders' required return — covered in the dividend decision.

Debentures are instruments for long-term borrowing, issued under a debenture trust deed, secured or unsecured, listed or unlisted, usually for 3–10 years. Interest is a tax-deductible expense, so debentures are the cheapest long-term source; investors prefer them to preference shares because interest is payable whether or not there is profit.

By convertibility: non-convertible (repaid at maturity), fully convertible (converted into equity on stated terms, so usually lower interest) and partly convertible. Other kinds: bearer, registered, mortgage (secured), naked/simple (unsecured), redeemable and irredeemable.

Merits: lowest cost, no dilution of control, attractive in inflation (fixed outgo falls in real terms). Demerits: interest and principal are compulsory; restrictive covenants; higher financial risk; large cash outflow at maturity. A public issue of debentures must be credit-rated (agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE).

Bonds are fixed-income securities raised by public issue or private placement. A callable bond lets the issuer redeem early at a call price; a puttable bond lets the investor sell it back early. Indian examples: masala bonds (rupee-denominated, issued abroad), municipal bonds (for urban infrastructure) and government/treasury bonds.
concepts.analogy: Retained earnings are your own savings — free of interest and of anyone else's say; debentures are a loan with a fixed EMI that you must pay even in a bad month.
concepts.work: Listed companies regularly raise money through non-convertible debentures (NCDs) rated by credit-rating agencies.

concepts.title: Term loans, bridge finance and venture capital
body: Term loans from financial institutions: national institutions (e.g. IFCI, SFCs, IDBI, ICICI — several later became banks) and international ones (World Bank/IBRD, IFC, ADB) provide long-term project finance.
Commercial banks, traditionally short-term lenders, now give long-term loans for expansion and fund the permanent (minimum) level of working capital through a working capital term loan (WCTL).

Bridge finance: a short-term bank loan taken while a sanctioned term loan awaits disbursement, so the project need not wait. It is repaid from the term loan when disbursed, is secured by movable assets and guarantees, and usually costs more than the term loan.

Venture capital: long-term, mainly equity finance for new, high-risk, growth-oriented ventures by qualified entrepreneurs who lack funds and experience. Besides money, the investor adds strategy, networking and management support.

Methods of venture financing: equity (the investor usually keeps a minority stake so control stays with the entrepreneur); conditional loan (no interest; repaid as a royalty on sales once sales begin); income note (low interest plus low royalty); participating debenture (no interest at start-up, low interest next, higher interest later).
concepts.analogy: Bridge finance is the temporary plank laid across a stream until the proper bridge (term loan) arrives; venture capital is a mentor who invests money as well as advice.
concepts.work: Indian start-ups raise "Series A/B" rounds from venture funds that take board seats and help with hiring and strategy.

concepts.title: Debt securitisation
body: Securitisation converts illiquid assets (such as loans) into marketable securities. The originator sells a pool of loans to a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV); the SPV pays the originator and issues securities to investors backed by the cash flows from the pool.
Benefits to the originator: immediate cash, loans move off the balance sheet, more lending capacity. Benefits to investors: a liquid investment in a diversified pool of loans.
The original borrowers usually continue paying as before and may not know of the transfer; their payments ultimately flow to the investors.
concepts.analogy: Securitisation is like selling your future rent receipts in a bundle today to get cash now — the buyer collects the rent later.
concepts.work: Vehicle-finance NBFCs in India regularly securitise their loan pools to raise funds.

concepts.title: Lease financing
body: Leasing is a contract under which the lessor buys an asset and lets the lessee use it for periodic rentals. It is an alternative to buying with own or borrowed money and can be arranged faster than term loans.

Operating lease: short period compared to the asset's life, usually cancellable, lessor bears maintenance, insurance and obsolescence and re-leases the asset to others — suits firms that want to keep updating equipment.

Financial (capital) lease: long-term, non-cancellable, covering most of the asset's useful life; lessee bears maintenance, insurance and obsolescence; the lessor is just a financier — effectively a loan in disguise.

Other leases: sale and lease back (owner sells the asset and leases it back — gets cash, keeps using it); leveraged lease (lessor borrows a large part of the cost from a lender, who is paid from rentals); sales-aid lease (lessor ties up with a manufacturer to market its products and earns from both); close-ended (asset returns to lessor) vs open-ended (lessee may buy at the end).
For the lessee, lease rentals are tax-deductible and there is no large immediate outflow; buying instead gives depreciation and deductible interest — so lease vs buy needs evaluation.
concepts.analogy: An operating lease is renting a car for a weekend trip; a financial lease is driving the same car for its whole life while paying the financier instalments.
concepts.work: Airlines commonly use sale and lease back to release cash tied up in aircraft.

concepts.title: Short-term sources and bank credit
body: Trade credit: credit from suppliers (often 15–90 days); arises automatically, has no explicit cost and grows with business volume — the most common short-term source.

Accrued expenses (wages, taxes not yet paid) and deferred income (advance receipts for future supplies) are spontaneous sources. Advances from customers, common in long manufacturing or construction contracts, are cost-free.

Money market instruments: commercial paper — an unsecured promissory note issued by highly rated companies (and certain other permitted issuers) under RBI rules, with a credit rating; treasury bills — short-term central government securities with maturities up to 364 days; certificates of deposit — negotiable time-deposit receipts issued by banks for a fixed period from 7 days to 1 year, tradable in the secondary market.

Bank credit takes several forms (table). Inter-corporate deposits are short-term loans from companies with surplus funds. Public deposits, accepted subject to legal limits, are unsecured and should finance working capital, not fixed assets.
concepts.analogy: Trade credit is the shop that lets you pay at the month end; cash credit is a credit card limit you draw and repay as needed and pay interest only on what you use.
concepts.work: Large FMCG companies keep working capital low by stretching supplier credit and collecting from customers quickly.

concepts.title: Export finance by banks
body: Banks give short-term export finance in rupees or foreign currency at two stages: pre-shipment and post-shipment.

Pre-shipment (packing credit): an advance to buy, make, process and pack goods against a firm export order or an irrevocable letter of credit; repaid from export proceeds within the period allowed (the study material uses 180 days). Types: clean packing credit (no charge on goods; ECGC cover obtained), against hypothecation of goods, against pledge of goods (bank holds the goods), with ECGC guarantee, and with a forward exchange contract to cover currency risk.

Post-shipment: purchase or discount of export bills backed by shipping documents; ECGC post-shipment guarantee; advances against bills sent for collection; advances against duty drawback or export incentives.
Other help from banks: opening letters of credit for exporters' purchases, issuing guarantees, financing deferred-payment exports, and providing status reports and market information.
concepts.analogy: Pre-shipment finance pays for getting the goods ready; post-shipment finance bridges the wait until the foreign buyer pays.
concepts.work: An exporter of garments typically uses packing credit to buy fabric and post-shipment bill discounting after dispatch.

concepts.title: Other, international and contemporary sources
body: Other sources: seed capital assistance for qualified entrepreneurs short of funds; internal cash accruals; unsecured loans from promoters (subordinate to institutional loans and treated as quasi-equity); deferred payment guarantee (supplier finances machinery against a bank guarantee); capital incentives/subsidies for backward areas (project must be viable without them).

Special bonds: deep discount and zero coupon bonds (issued at a discount, redeemed at face value — the discount is the interest); secured premium notes with detachable warrants; zero-interest fully convertible debentures; option bonds; inflation-indexed bonds; floating rate bonds; high-yield (junk) bonds rated below investment grade.

International sources: foreign currency loans from banks and development banks, international agencies (IFC, IBRD, ADB), and capital markets — external commercial borrowings (automatic and approval routes), euro bonds (issued in a currency other than that of the country of issue), foreign bonds (in the currency of the country of issue), fully hedged bonds, medium-term notes, floating rate notes, euro commercial paper, euro convertible bonds, and ESG bonds (green, social, sustainability-linked).
Depository receipts: ADRs (listed in the US), GDRs (mainly European markets) and IDRs (foreign companies raising money in India).
Contemporary sources: crowdfunding through online platforms — equity crowdfunding, peer-to-peer (P2P) lending, and donation-based funding.
concepts.analogy: Finance today is a buffet — from a promoter's own loan to a green bond in London to a thousand small investors online.
concepts.work: Indian companies have raised money through masala bonds, green bonds and sustainability-linked bonds in recent years.

illustrations.title: Equity, debentures or preference shares — effect on EPS
illustrations.q: Nilgiri Foods Ltd. has 4,00,000 equity shares and no debt. It needs ₹50,00,000 for expansion, after which EBIT is expected to be ₹40,00,000. Tax rate 25%. Options: (A) issue 1,00,000 equity shares at ₹50; (B) issue 12% debentures; (C) issue 11% preference shares. Compute EPS under each plan and comment.

solution.text: Debentures give the highest EPS (₹6.38) because interest is tax-deductible and no new shares are issued. Preference shares avoid dilution but their dividend is paid from after-tax profit, so EPS (₹6.12) is lower than with debt. Equity gives the lowest EPS (₹6) but adds no fixed burden — a choice to make when business risk is high.
Higher EPS with debt comes with higher financial risk: interest and repayment are compulsory.

checks.label: Plan C (11% preference): profit for equity

illustrations.title: Pricing a deep discount (zero-interest) bond
illustrations.q: A company issues deep discount bonds of face value ₹1,00,000 redeemable at par after 5 years, with no periodic interest. Investors want a 10% annual return. At what price should each bond be issued, and what is the investor's total return?

solution.text: The investor pays ₹62,092 and receives ₹1,00,000 after 5 years — a gain of ₹37,908, which is the interest earned. The company has no cash outgo until maturity, which suits projects with a long gestation period.

jobs.title: Choosing finance for a new plant
jobs.situation: A profitable mid-sized company needs ₹80 crore for a plant with a 2-year construction period; promoters do not want to lose control.
steps: Match a long-term need with long-term sources — term loan and debentures plus some internal accruals.
Avoid fresh equity to protect control; consider convertible instruments only if control can be preserved.
Arrange bridge finance if the term-loan disbursement will be delayed; compare EPS and risk under each mix.
jobs.takeaway: Match maturity, protect control and keep financial risk within limits.

jobs.title: Lease or buy for IT equipment
jobs.situation: Laptops become obsolete within three years; the company has limited cash.
steps: Prefer an operating lease — obsolescence risk stays with the lessor.
Compare total rentals with the cost of buying net of tax benefits.
jobs.takeaway: For fast-ageing assets, an operating lease shifts obsolescence risk away.

mcqs.q: The basic principle of financing is that:
options: Long-term needs should be met from long-term sources and short-term needs from short-term sources
All needs should be met from equity
All needs should be met from bank overdraft
Short-term needs should be met from long-term sources only
mcqs.explain: Funds should match the period for which they are needed: fixed assets and core working capital from long-term sources, seasonal working capital from short-term sources. Funding long-term assets with short-term loans creates refinancing risk. In practice: lenders check this matching when appraising projects.

mcqs.q: Which source of long-term finance usually has the highest cost?
mcqs.explain: Equity shareholders bear the highest risk — they are paid last and have no fixed return — so they expect the highest return, making equity the costliest source. Debentures are cheapest because interest is tax-deductible. In practice: companies with stable cash flows use more debt to lower overall cost.

mcqs.q: Preference share capital is called hybrid because:
options: Its dividend is fixed like debt interest but not tax-deductible like equity dividend
mcqs.explain: Preference shares resemble debt in having a fixed rate of return and equity in that the dividend is an appropriation of profit, not a tax-deductible expense. They are not always convertible and carry only limited voting rights. In practice: this is why they cost more than debentures.

mcqs.q: Debentures are the cheapest source of long-term finance mainly because:
mcqs.explain: Debenture interest is deducted before tax, so the effective cost is lower, and investors accept a lower return because debt is safer. They have no voting rights and must be repaid on maturity. In practice: at 25% tax, 12% interest costs the company only 9% after tax.

mcqs.q: A bond that gives the issuer the right to redeem it before maturity is a:
mcqs.explain: A callable bond has a call option for the issuer to redeem early at a stated call price, usually at a premium. A puttable bond gives the investor the right to sell it back early. In practice: issuers call bonds when interest rates fall, refinancing at lower cost.

mcqs.q: A masala bond is:
options: A rupee-denominated bond issued outside India
A dollar bond issued in India
A bond issued by a municipal body
mcqs.explain: Masala bonds are issued in overseas markets but denominated in Indian rupees, so the currency risk is borne by the foreign investor, not the Indian issuer. Municipal and treasury bonds are domestic instruments. In practice: large Indian companies used masala bonds to tap foreign investors without currency risk.

mcqs.q: Bridge finance refers to:
options: A short-term loan taken pending disbursement of a sanctioned term loan
A loan for building a bridge
mcqs.explain: Bridge finance is a short-term bank loan that lets the project proceed while the term loan already sanctioned awaits disbursement; it is repaid from the term loan. Its interest rate is usually higher than the term loan. In practice: it avoids costly delays in starting construction.
mcqs.topic: Term loans, bridge finance and venture capital

mcqs.q: Under a conditional loan in venture capital financing:
options: No interest is charged; repayment is by royalty on sales
Interest is charged at a fixed high rate from day one
The investor takes a majority stake
The loan is repayable on demand
mcqs.explain: A conditional loan carries no interest; it is repaid as a royalty on sales once the venture starts selling, matching repayment to success. An income note combines low interest with low royalty. In practice: such terms protect a start-up's cash flow in its early years.
mcqs.topic: Term loans, bridge finance and venture capital

mcqs.q: In securitisation, the entity that buys the pool of loans and issues securities is the:
mcqs.explain: The originator sells the loan pool to a Special Purpose Vehicle, which issues securities to investors backed by the pool's cash flows. Rating agencies may rate the securities but do not buy the loans. In practice: this lets lenders raise cash and move loans off their balance sheet.

mcqs.q: In a financial lease, the risk of obsolescence is borne by the:
mcqs.explain: A financial lease transfers the risks and rewards of ownership to the lessee, including obsolescence, maintenance and insurance; the lessor is merely a financier. In an operating lease the lessor bears obsolescence. In practice: firms lease fast-changing technology on operating leases for this reason.

mcqs.q: Under sale and lease back:
options: The owner sells an asset and takes it back on lease
The lessor borrows most of the asset cost from a lender
The lessor ties up with a manufacturer to market products
The lessee must buy the asset at the end
mcqs.explain: In sale and lease back, the owner sells the asset to raise cash and immediately leases it back, continuing to use it. Borrowing most of the cost from a lender describes a leveraged lease; a manufacturer tie-up describes a sales-aid lease. In practice: it releases capital locked in buildings or aircraft.

mcqs.q: Under a cash credit arrangement, interest is charged on:
options: The average of the limit and the drawing
mcqs.explain: In cash credit the borrower draws only as needed within the sanctioned limit, and interest is charged on the amount actually used. Paying interest on the full limit would defeat the flexibility of the facility. In practice: businesses deposit surplus cash into the account to cut interest cost.

mcqs.q: Commercial paper is:
options: An unsecured short-term promissory note issued by highly rated borrowers
A deposit certificate issued by banks
mcqs.explain: Commercial paper is an unsecured money-market instrument in the form of a promissory note, issued by creditworthy borrowers with a credit rating under RBI rules. Certificates of deposit are issued by banks and treasury bills by the government. In practice: large companies use CP to borrow cheaper than bank loans.

mcqs.q: Packing credit is a form of:
mcqs.explain: Packing credit is advanced before shipment to buy, process and pack goods for export against a firm order or letter of credit. Discounting export bills after dispatch is post-shipment finance. In practice: the advance is repaid from the export proceeds when the foreign buyer pays.

mcqs.q: A zero coupon bond:
options: Pays no periodic interest and is issued at a discount to face value
mcqs.explain: A zero coupon bond pays no periodic interest; it is issued below face value and redeemed at face value, the difference being the investor's return. Inflation-linked interest describes inflation bonds. In practice: such bonds suit projects that generate cash only after several years.

mcqs.q: GDRs are mainly traded in:
mcqs.explain: Global Depository Receipts are negotiable certificates representing shares of a company, mainly traded in European markets such as London; ADRs are listed in the US and IDRs in India. In practice: many Indian companies chose GDRs because US listing brings heavier disclosure duties.

mcqs.q: Peer-to-peer (P2P) lending is a form of:
options: Crowdfunding where lenders give loans to borrowers through an online platform
mcqs.explain: P2P lending matches individual lenders with borrowers through an online platform; the loans are repaid with interest and carry default risk. Equity crowdfunding gives investors shares, and donation-based funding expects no return. In practice: P2P platforms in India are regulated by the RBI.

mcqs.q: Using the Nilgiri Foods data (EBIT ₹40,00,000, tax 25%, 4,00,000 existing shares, ₹50,00,000 needed), EPS under 12% debentures is:
mcqs.explain: Interest = 12% × 50,00,000 = 6,00,000; PBT = 34,00,000; tax 8,50,000; PAT 25,50,000; EPS = 25,50,000 ÷ 4,00,000 = ₹6.38. The equity plan gives ₹6 because shares rise to 5,00,000. In practice: debt raises EPS when the return on funds exceeds the after-tax cost of debt.

questions.q: Explain the methods of venture capital financing.

items: Equity financing: long-term equity contribution, kept to a minority stake so that control remains with the entrepreneur.
Conditional loan: no interest; repaid as a royalty on sales once the venture generates sales.
Income note: a hybrid — the entrepreneur pays both interest and royalty, at low rates.
Participating debenture: no interest in the start-up phase, a low rate in the next phase and a higher rate thereafter.

remarks: Four methods, one line each, is enough.
mistakes: Confusing income note with conditional loan.

model.text: Debentures give the highest EPS (₹6.38) because interest is tax-deductible and no new shares are issued. Preference shares avoid dilution but their dividend is paid from after-tax profit, so EPS (₹6.12) is lower than with debt. Equity gives the lowest EPS (₹6) but adds no fixed burden — a choice to make when business risk is high.
Higher EPS with debt comes with higher financial risk: interest and repayment are compulsory.

summary: Match maturity: long-term needs from long-term sources, short-term from short-term.
Cost ranking (usual): equity > preference > debt; debt interest is tax-deductible.
Preference shares are hybrid; debentures are long-term debt under a trust deed.
Bridge finance covers the gap until a sanctioned term loan is disbursed.
Venture capital: equity, conditional loan, income note, participating debenture.
Financial lease = loan in disguise; operating lease = rental, lessor bears obsolescence.
Export finance: pre-shipment (packing credit) and post-shipment (bills).
remember: Euro bond: currency ≠ country of issue; foreign bond: currency = country of issue.
ADR — US; GDR — mainly Europe; IDR — India.
traps: Cash credit interest is on the amount used, not the limit.
Preference dividend is paid from after-tax profit.

viva.q: Why is preference share capital called a hybrid source?
viva.model: Because its dividend is at a fixed rate like interest on debt, but the dividend is not tax deductible and is paid out of profits like equity dividend.

cases.title: Funding plan at Rangoli Textiles
cases.case: Rangoli Textiles, an exporter, plans a ₹30 crore weaving unit. A term loan is sanctioned but disbursement will take four months. It also needs funds to buy yarn for a confirmed US order, and wants to replace computers every three years. Promoters wish to keep control.

mcqs.q: To start construction without waiting four months, Rangoli should use:
mcqs.explain: Bridge finance is a short-term bank loan taken pending disbursement of a sanctioned term loan and repaid from it. Trade credit and commercial paper are working-capital tools. In practice: bridge loans usually cost a little more than the term loan.
mcqs.topic: Term loans, bridge finance and venture capital

mcqs.q: Funds to buy yarn for the confirmed export order are best raised through:
mcqs.explain: Packing credit is pre-shipment finance to buy, process and pack goods against a firm export order or letter of credit. Bill discounting is post-shipment finance given after dispatch. In practice: it is repaid from the export proceeds.

mcqs.q: For computers replaced every three years, the more suitable arrangement is:
mcqs.explain: An operating lease keeps obsolescence risk with the lessor and is usually cancellable, ideal for equipment that becomes outdated quickly. A financial lease would put the obsolescence risk on Rangoli. In practice: IT equipment is often taken on operating leases.

mcqs.q: To fund the unit without diluting promoters' control, Rangoli should prefer:
options: A fresh public issue of equity
mcqs.explain: Debt (term loans and debentures) carries no voting rights, so control is not diluted, and interest is tax-deductible. A fresh equity issue brings new voting shareholders. In practice: the trade-off is higher financial risk from fixed interest and repayment.
